factsfirstdaily.preview_text: Nvidia investors back a slow CEO search, a Starship first and a NATO idea for Ukraine.

stories.title: The US Loses Its Measles Elimination Status After 26 Years

photo.alt: A hand holds a syringe and a flu vaccine vial; illustrative file photo.

paragraphs: The United States has lost its measles elimination status. NPR reports the Pan American Health Organization concluded measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. Researchers with direct knowledge of the decision told KFF Health News.
The U.S. had held the status since 2000. CBS News reports the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases so far in 2026. That is more than double last year's total of 2,242 cases.
The CDC counts at least six measles deaths this year. Some states report more. Al Jazeera reports Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced another measles associated death on Friday.

Why it matters. Measles can now spread in ongoing chains among unvaccinated people. CBS News reports PAHO says a vaccination rate of 95% or higher is the best protection. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.

stories.title: Two Big Nvidia Investors Urge the Board to Keep Huang's Return on the Table

photo.alt: Network equipment in a server rack; illustrative file photo, not Nvidia hardware.

paragraphs: Two large Nvidia shareholders asked the chipmaker's board to take its time choosing a new chief executive. CNBC reports Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker want the search to leave room for Jensen Huang's return.

Huang resigned Thursday after reports about personal relationships. An independent board investigation is underway. The letter did not call for his immediate reinstatement. It said interim chief Colette Kress can capably lead the company.
The two firms disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock combined as of June 30. CNBC reports Elon Musk said he signed a petition to reinstate Huang.

Why it matters. Nvidia sits at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. CNBC reports some fund managers say Big Tech rivals could gain if buyers lose trust in Nvidia. Wedbush analyst Dan Ives still sees chip demand outrunning supply.

stories.title: SpaceX Catches the Upper Stage of Starship for the First Time

photo.alt: A stainless steel rocket stands beside a launch tower; file photo.

paragraphs: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with mechanical arms on its launch tower Saturday. CNBC reports it was the first catch of the spacecraft returning from orbit. The catch happened at Starbase, Texas.

The ship circled Earth 14 times before landing in the tower's arms. BBC News reports SpaceX called the landing picture perfect. The booster catch was called off Friday, and it exploded above the Gulf of Mexico.
During the flight, SpaceX released 26 new Starlink satellites. CNBC reports the company's constellation already includes over 11,000 satellites.

Why it matters. A reusable Starship could cut launch costs and speed satellite deployment. NASA is counting on Starship to carry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface. Flight 15 was the first try at catching both stages.

stories.title: Zelenskyy Says US Floated Trading Donbas for NATO Membership

photo.alt: The Independence Monument column on Maidan Nezalezhnosti in Kyiv; file photo.

paragraphs: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says U.S. negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine leaving Donbas in exchange for joining NATO. NBC News reports he called it the first time the link had come up.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv is not ready to give up land. BBC News reports a U.S. official said many ideas are still being discussed. Any deal would need both sides to agree.

Zelenskyy said he would put a full package to a national referendum. It would need security guarantees, a strong army and rebuilding funds. Politico reports he said there would be no recognition of occupied land as Russian.
Why it matters. Russia has long called Ukrainian NATO membership a red line. BBC News reports other NATO members are also wary of admitting Ukraine. Russia controls most of the Donbas region.

deep_dive.title: What Israel's Killing of a Hamas Commander Means for the Gaza Truce

photo.alt: A family sits in a makeshift tent among damaged buildings; file photo.

paragraphs: An Israeli airstrike killed the commander of Hamas's Rafah Brigade in southern Gaza on Saturday. BBC News reports Samir Abu Younis was killed in the Al-Mawasi area. Hamas confirmed his death.

What happened. Eyewitnesses said four missiles hit a tent in a camp sheltering hundreds of displaced people. Al Jazeera reports the strike wounded two others. Israel's military said it took steps to limit harm to civilians.

The backstory. Hamas's armed wing called Younis one of the key planners of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack. He had led the brigade since Sept. 15. He took over after the death of the previous commander. Al Jazeera reports Israel had designated Al-Mawasi a humanitarian zone but has struck it repeatedly.

What comes next. A ceasefire took effect on Oct. 11, 2025. Strikes have continued since then. Gaza's Health Ministry says Israeli attacks killed 16 people over 48 hours. It counts at least 1,643 Palestinians killed since the truce began. Cold related deaths have risen to 11, including a baby who died of hypothermia. Most residents, many of them displaced, live in tents or damaged buildings after recent heavy rains. Hamas said Younis's funeral would be held Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis.

trivia.question: Since what year had the United States held measles elimination status?
trivia.explanation: C. 2000. CBS News reports the country was declared measles free that year.

World view: ASEAN leaders open Manila summit. Trump is expected to join a special summit with the bloc on Nov. 17 as oil shortages hit the region; Al Jazeera reports.
Iraq fires nine officials over smuggling. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed security officers after a probe found illegal oil refineries; Al Jazeera reports.
Need to know: Airlines expect a full recovery Sunday. The FAA chief said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious behind Friday's ground stop; ABC News reports.
Flight cancellations ran into Saturday. More than 5,000 flights were canceled Saturday after Friday's nationwide halt, FlightAware data show; CBS News reports.
Money & markets: Canadian stocks gain since the midterms. The TSX is up 1.6% since the vote as investors bet on softer U.S. trade policy; CNBC reports.
Family offices bet small on startups. Megadeals made up 87.5% of U.S. venture funding in early 2026, but some investors favor younger firms; CNBC reports.
Future frontiers: Migraine visions under study. Lancaster University scientists are in a four year study of why migraines can trigger hallucinations; BBC News reports.
Data center doubts weigh on AI. Wedbush's Dan Ives says 10% to 20% of planned data centers may not be built under a Democratic Congress; CNBC reports.
The score: Kentucky playoff hopes fade. The No. 11 Wildcats lost 21-14 to unranked Florida, and LSU fell 22-21 to Texas; CBS Sports reports.
Iowa State routs Cincinnati. Aiden Flora ran for 216 yards and three touchdowns in a 41-13 Cyclones win; CBS Sports reports.
Life & culture: Bands play for stranded flyers. Simple Plan, Hoobastank and The Used sang their hits over plane PA systems during the travel delays; ABC News reports.
Cunk turns to cinema. Philomena Cunk's new film series tops the week's best reviewed culture picks; The Guardian reports.

stories.title: Officials Blame a Contractor Router for the Nationwide Flight Shutdown

photo.alt: Air traffic control tower at dusk; file photo, 2022.

paragraphs: Reuters reports officials said a single router installed by contractor L3Harris may have caused Friday's nearly five-hour aviation shutdown. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the router flooded other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Officials have not yet determined the fault.

CNBC reports nearly 6,500 US flights were canceled Saturday as of 9 p.m. ET, after more than 9,000 on Friday. Al Jazeera reports the FAA expects full schedule integrity by the end of Sunday. FAA chief Bryan Bedford said he saw zero evidence of anything nefarious.

stories.title: Judge Blocks Trump From Closing a Historic Washington Golf Course for Now

photo.alt: Tidal Basin in Washington; file photo, 2026.

paragraphs: A federal judge on Saturday blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park and its public golf course. AP reports Judge Ana Reyes ordered a two-week delay to any work, a day before the course was due to close for 15 months. The order runs through Nov. 28.

NBC News reports the paths and course must stay open to the public while the case moves forward. Reyes doubted the government's safety argument, noting crews cut down more than 400 trees within 10 days. The Justice Department said planning for a world-class course can continue.

stories.title: SpaceX Catches a Returning Starship in Its Launch Tower Arms

photo.alt: SpaceX Starbase launch site, Texas; file photo, 2026.

paragraphs: AP reports Starship was caught in midair by the arms of its launch tower on Saturday, about 22 hours after liftoff. It was the first capture of a Starship flying back from space. The booster exploded shortly after Friday's launch, so SpaceX missed its hoped-for double catch.

SpaceX says the ship deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites after reaching orbit. The booster's boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass, and the cause is under investigation. NASA is paying billions for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade.

stories.title: Zelenskyy Says the US Asked About Trading Donbas for NATO Membership

photo.alt: Ukrainian flag on a flagpole; file photo, 2025.

paragraphs: NBC News reports US negotiators floated Ukraine withdrawing from Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said it was the first time talks had linked NATO membership to territory. The idea came up after the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi.

AP reports Zelenskyy said Kyiv would not surrender its territory and would not recognize occupied land as Russian. He said a full package of security guarantees, military strength and recovery funds could go to a national referendum. He also rejected neutrality, saying it would require a constitutional change.

deep_dive.title: What Losing Measles Elimination Status Means for American Families

photo.alt: Health worker filling a syringe; file photo, 2021.

paragraphs: What happened. CBS News reports the United States has lost its measles elimination status, a decision by the Pan American Health Organization. The country recorded more than 5,400 cases this year, more than double last year's total. It is the first time since 2000 that the country missed the standard. PAHO plans a news conference on Tuesday.

Why it matters. The CDC has counted 5,412 cases, more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths this year. Reuters reports Wisconsin confirmed the death of a second child linked to its outbreak. Pennsylvania reported its seventh death, an unvaccinated Montour County resident. The state has recorded 1,542 cases in 46 counties.

What each side says. CBS medical correspondent Dr. Celine Gounder said unvaccinated people are now at risk of exposure. She said doctors should consider measles in anyone with fever and rash. Epidemiologist Dr. Omer Awan called the loss frustrating and heartbreaking. He noted the MMR vaccine is 97% effective at preventing measles, CBS reports.

What comes next. PAHO says keeping vaccination at 95% or higher is the best way to maintain elimination. Regaining the status requires no local spread or outbreaks lasting more than a year. Gounder noted states set school vaccine rules, and most legislatures reconvene in January. CBS reports nine states made opting out easier in 2025.

World view: Quad leaders plan a Manila meeting. Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet Tuesday, their first summit in two years; Reuters reports.
Carney cites trade progress. The Canadian prime minister said he held lengthy talks with Trump but the two sides have no deal yet; Reuters reports.
Hungary eases abortion rules. Prime Minister Peter Magyar said emergency contraception will be easier to get under a women's rights package; Reuters reports.
COP31 enters its final week. The UN climate chief urged negotiators in Turkey to move swiftly toward a deal and avoid tactical delays; Reuters reports.
Need to know: New York is sued over warning labels. NetChoice says a state law requiring warnings on addictive social media features violates the First Amendment; Reuters reports.
Illinois lifts a bomb-threat evacuation. Bomb technicians made safe a device found near an ethanol plant in Peoria after a 1-mile evacuation; Reuters reports.
Jeffries is heckled in Denver. About 10 protesters accused the incoming House speaker of being too timid on the cost of living; Reuters reports.
The government drops an ICE app fight. Free speech group FIRE said officials agreed to stop pressing Apple and Facebook over platforms tracking ICE activity; Reuters reports.
Money & markets: CVS sets a GLP-1 break-even price. Health plans could break even on the drugs at below $350 a month as medical spending falls; Reuters reports.
Windward Bio debuts at $1 billion. The Novo Holdings-backed company's shares opened at $18.35 after an IPO priced at $17; Reuters reports.
AstraZeneca cuts 600 US jobs. The sales cuts are part of a plan to save about $1.5 billion a year, Bloomberg News reported; Reuters reports.
Indonesia wants more from mining. President Prabowo Subianto said at least 70% of benefits from mining permits must go to the state; Reuters reports.
Future frontiers: Voyager 1 nears a light-day away. NASA says the probe will reach about 16 billion miles from Earth on Wednesday morning; Reuters reports.
The Wegovy pill shows real-world results. Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk's daily pill lost an average of 6.2% of body weight in three months; Reuters reports.
Lilly shares new obesity data. The drugmaker released early trial results at the ObesityWeek conference but has not released full results; Reuters reports.
The EU nears a new blood pressure pill. A European panel backed AstraZeneca's baxdrostat for patients whose hypertension resists two other medicines; Reuters reports.
The score: Andreeva reaches the WTA Finals title match. The Russian teenager beat Jessica Pegula 6-3 6-4 and will face Elina Svitolina; AP reports.
Jeremiah Smith sets a Big Ten record. The Ohio State receiver broke the conference mark for career receiving yards against Northwestern; Reuters reports.
The NFL swaps referees after the shutdown. Three Week 10 games went to backup referees who live within driving distance; Reuters reports.
Ole Miss and Oklahoma move to Sunday. The SEC rescheduled the game over travel problems, and Oklahoma's athletic director objected; Reuters reports.
Life & culture: King Charles jokes with Elton John. The monarch said they were still standing in a radio clip aired on his 78th birthday; Reuters reports.
Pope Leo draws crowds in Argentina. Young Argentines packed Buenos Aires parks to hear him promise a church open to everyone; AP reports.
A student pilot gets a surprise. He was on his first solo cross-country flight when a controller told him to land during the ground stop; Reuters reports.
Lahore fights smog with a fire squad. A new Pakistani unit is racing to put out illegal stubble fires blamed for the haze; Reuters reports.

stories.title: Houthis Take Control Near a Key Red Sea Strait as Yemen Forces Pull Back
paragraphs: Yemeni forces backing the Saudi-supported government said on Sunday they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Reuters reports that the move leaves the Iran-aligned Houthis in control. The southern forces said they were redeploying toward Aden to protect the government seat.

The strait is one of the busiest routes for shipping between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. Reuters says the shift gives the Houthis more leverage while Iran disrupts the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters also reports that the Saudi-led coalition intercepted two Houthi missiles fired toward Riyadh on Sunday.

stories.title: Israeli Strike Kills a Senior Hamas Commander in Southern Gaza
paragraphs: An Israeli airstrike has killed Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed head of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade, officials on both sides said. The BBC reports that he helped plan and oversee the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Witnesses said missiles hit a tent in a camp for displaced people in Al-Mawasi.

The Israeli military said it took steps to limit harm to civilians before the strike. Hamas called the killing a cowardly assassination. Reuters reports that Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed in that time.

photo.alt: Damaged buildings in Gaza City, 2025 file photo

stories.title: Canada Pledges Up to C$560 Million for a Brazil-Led Forest Fund
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney met Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva at the Asean summit in Manila on Sunday. Ottawa says Canada will give up to C$560 million over four years to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility. Brazil and Norway co-lead the fund, which pays countries to protect tropical forests.

A Canadian government backgrounder says the money comes as a loan from its existing climate finance envelope. At least 20% of conservation payments must go to Indigenous Peoples and local communities. The World Bank serves as trustee, and Luxembourg will host the investment arm. Payments depend on verified conservation results.

deep_dive.title: Italy Fines Meta $887 Million Over Facebook Access to Phone Photos
paragraphs: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta 805 million euros, or about $887 million. The BBC reports that Meta accessed Android users’ photos and videos without their specific consent. The regulator says about 20 million smartphone users in Italy were not properly informed. The case centres on a Facebook feature that suggests gallery photos as ideas for posts.

The Guardian reports that the fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech company. The regulator said Facebook used a single app-wide permission with a vague notice. Users could not tell they were also allowing gallery suggestions. It also cited the number of people affected and Meta’s lack of cooperation.

Meta told the BBC it strongly disagrees with the regulator’s assessment of the facts and the law. It says it will appeal, and the company calls the fine disproportionate. It says users must give permission on their device before the feature works. Meta also says people can change that permission at any time in their settings. The ruling follows a $25 billion penalty in New Mexico last month.

CNBC reports that Meta has 60 days to switch the feature off by default and seek consent separately. The investigation did not cover whether the content was used to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies. The authority reserved the right to assess separately a newer feature that processes gallery content in the cloud. The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta’s global revenue.
